metadata.note: The Denver & Rio Grande's narrow-gauge (3ft) branch from Durango to Silverton, CO, built to reach the San Juan Mountains mining district. Construction began July 1881 and the first train reached Silverton in July 1882. Unlike almost every other D&RG narrow-gauge branch, this line has never lost all service since: as other narrow-gauge lines were progressively abandoned through the 20th century, this one instead grew into a scenic tourist showcase, and it still operates today as a heritage railroad. Drawn here as four features sharing identical geometry, split at each real change in operator and (for the D&RGW era) at the best-documented point where the line's own character shifted from ordinary transportation to a tourist excursion product: (1) Denver & Rio Grande Railway, 1882-1921; (2) Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad as ordinary mixed/passenger service, 1921-1946; (3) the same D&RGW company, now run as a tourist excursion (mode tourist_rail) from the 1947 launch of the dedicated summer excursion 'The Silverton' through the last D&RGW-operated train on October 5 1980; (4) the Durango & Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad, the private heritage operator that bought the line in March 1981 and has run it continuously since (through further changes of corporate ownership in 1997 and 1998 that did not change the operating brand, so those are not drawn as further splits). TOURIST-ERA JUDGMENT CALL: the mode switch to tourist_rail is placed at 1947 rather than 1981, because the best-documented milestones (the 1947 launch of a dedicated summer excursion train, the 1960s ICC abandonment petitions rejected specifically because of 'continued increase in tourist patronage,' and the 1966 National Register of Historic Places listing) show the line's primary character as a scenic attraction well before the 1981 change of corporate ownership -- the sale did not create the tourist era, it privatized an operation that was already tourist-driven. The line continued to carry some general freight/mail alongside excursion traffic as a 'mixed train' into the 1950s-60s; this is noted in the segment text rather than changing the drawn years, per CLAUDE.md's passenger-service test. COLOR NOTE / KNOWN CONFLICT: per this task's instructions this file uses #8B5E3C for the pre-1921 Denver & Rio Grande Railway (matching data/denver_early_railroads.geojson and data/drgw_royal_gorge_route.geojson) and #B5451B for the 1921-1981 Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad era, per an explicit instruction that #B5451B is a color newly reserved for D&RGW across a same-day multi-agent build-out. AT THE TIME THIS FILE WAS WRITTEN, NEITHER OF THE TWO OTHER EXISTING D&RGW FEATURES IN data/ ACTUALLY USED #B5451B: data/drgw_royal_gorge_route.geojson colors its whole 'Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad' feature #8B5E3C (the D&RG Railway's own color -- itself an apparent same-company-same-color bug, since it also fails to split at the 1921 reorganization the way this file does), and data/denver_early_railroads.geojson colors its D&RGW feature #B5451B. #B5451B was ALSO already in use, unrelated to D&RGW, by NJ Transit Rail (data/nj_transit_rail.geojson) and the Southern New York Railway (data/southern_new_york_railway.geojson). This file follows the task's explicit instruction rather than CLAUDE.md Rule 4's default 'reuse the existing color' procedure, on the understanding that a later cross-file integration pass reconciles all Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad features (and the NJ Transit / Southern New York Railway collision) to one consistent color; this note flags the conflict explicitly rather than silently picking a color, per CLAUDE.md Rule 3's spirit. The 1981-present Durango and Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad is given a brand-new color, #3E46B2, chosen programmatically (max-min RGB distance search over the full existing data/ palette of 214 unique colors) to avoid colliding with any color already in use anywhere in data/.

geometry_sources: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap via the Overpass API (https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter): route relation 3343191 ('Durango & Silverton Historic Train Route', route=train, historic=yes, passenger=local) and its 22 constituent railway=narrow_gauge member ways, all tagged name='Durango & Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad'. Nodes were snapped to 5 decimal places, assembled into a routing graph, and connected with a haversine-weighted Dijkstra shortest path between the depot-area endpoints in Durango, CO (37.27577, -107.88097) and Silverton, CO (37.81101, -107.6634). The resulting path is a single connected trace, 72.67 km (45.17 mi) long, against a documented mileage of 45.2 mi (72.75 km, per Wikipedia/Colorado Encyclopedia) -- a match within about 0.1%, as expected for a heritage line whose full original alignment survives intact and in active use. Checked for router self-intersection/backtracking (e.g. an out-and-back detour onto a dead-end spur or siding) using CUMULATIVE ALONG-PATH DISTANCE rather than point index: for all point pairs at least 500m apart along the traced path, direct (great-circle) distance was computed and any pair under 250m flagged for inspection. Zero pairs were flagged across all ~1340 traced points, so no backtrack artifact is present.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: Exact frequency/timetable for any era is unsourced and estimated; sources give the 1947 excursion launch date and a 1966 NRHP listing but not a precise year for when mixed/freight traffic alongside the tourist train fully ended. The exact 1981 sale date varies slightly by source (some cite March 25 1981, others only 'March 1981, during Durango's centennial'); this file uses 'March 1981' and does not assert the specific day. Whether there was a literal service gap between the October 5 1980 last D&RGW train and the start of Bradshaw-era service in 1981 is not confirmed either way -- both eras are seasonal (summer) operations, so a normal winter off-season gap is expected regardless of ownership, and this file does not draw a gap year for that reason. The unresolved D&RGW color conflict described in the top-level note is also unresolved as of this writing.

segments.note: The Denver & Rio Grande Railway built this branch from Durango to reach the San Juan Mountains' silver and gold mines; construction began July 1881 and the first train reached Silverton in July 1882, completing the 45.2-mile narrow-gauge line in about nine months. Ran as ordinary D&RG mixed/passenger/ore service until the railroad's August 1, 1921 bankruptcy reorganization as the Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad. Frequency estimated (once-daily mixed train assumed), unsourced.

segments.note: The D&RGW launched a dedicated summer-only passenger excursion, 'The Silverton' (the colorful 'Painted Train'), on June 24 1947, and by the 1950s the branch ran as a mixed train combining this excursion traffic with residual freight/mail. Tourist ridership, not general transportation, was by then the line's economic reason for existing: the ICC rejected D&RGW abandonment petitions in the 1960s specifically because of 'continued increase in tourist patronage,' forcing further D&RGW investment, and the line was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1966. Drawn here as tourist_rail from 1947 (rather than only from the 1981 change of ownership) because the operation's character -- a scenic excursion product -- was already established under the D&RGW; the 1981 sale privatized an already-tourist-driven railroad rather than creating the tourist era. The last D&RGW-operated train ran October 5, 1980. Frequency estimated (summer-season daily service, growing over the period), unsourced.

properties.speed_source: sourced: modern schedules cite a roughly 3.5-hour one-way run for the 45.2-mile (72.7km) route (e.g. 9:00am Durango departure, 12:30pm Silverton arrival), giving ~21 km/h average including station stops; durango.org and mild2wildrafting.com trip-planning pages

segments.note: Florida citrus grower Charles Bradshaw Jr. bought the branch from the D&RGW in March 1981, during Durango's centennial celebration, and incorporated it as the Durango & Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad Company. He sold it in 1997 to First American Railways, which sold it in 1998 to Allen and Carol Harper's American Heritage Railways, the current owner -- the operating brand 'Durango & Silverton Narrow Gauge Railroad' has stayed the same throughout, so no further split is drawn for those corporate ownership changes. Steam-powered, coal-fired trains still run the full 45.2-mile route to Silverton in summer (May-October) and a shortened run to Cascade Wye in winter, making this one of the very few former D&RG narrow-gauge lines that has never had a lapse in passenger service since 1882. Frequency estimated (multiple daily departures in peak season, varying by year and season; only a single representative 9am departure time is directly sourced), unsourced beyond that.
